news.article_content_en:
In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”

In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.

Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.

A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.)

The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.

Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows , has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack , arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. A representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication.

Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.

But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”

In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies .

For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.

“There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. “So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”

news.author: Reece Rogers
news.content_snippet:
I squint my eyes in confusion when Anton Osika asks if I like cakes. The CEO of Lovable was in the middle of explaining how his AI startup, flush with investment cash and recently valued at over $13 billion, is ready to shift its focus after two years. Why does the vibe-coding king care if I like sweet treats? He thinks that if I do, I might be able to vibe code a living out of that.

The generative AI revolution completely flipped coding. Rather than a niche skill set where humans had to learn
news.summary_en: Lovable CEO Anton Osika and CTO Fabian Hedin announced a strategic pivot for their $13B-valued startup, evolving their 'vibe coding' platform into an automated business management engine. With 80% of users seeking financial gain but only 35% currently monetizing, the company aims to bridge this gap by integrating automated business strategy, web development, and customer retention tools.
news.article_content_en:
I squint my eyes in confusion when Anton Osika asks if I like cakes. The CEO of Lovable was in the middle of explaining how his AI startup, flush with investment cash and recently valued at over $13 billion, is ready to shift its focus after two years. Why does the vibe-coding king care if I like sweet treats? He thinks that if I do, I might be able to vibe code a living out of that.

The generative AI revolution completely flipped coding. Rather than a niche skill set where humans had to learn how to talk like computers, software development could be done by computers generating code in response to natural-language requests from humans.

Osika was early to this shift, launching a viral open-source tool in 2023, a precursor to Lovable. His mission? “Reduce barriers to build.” That initial spark ignited what is now one of Europe’s most dynamic startups.

Tech insiders talked nonstop last year about the transformative power of “vibe coding” that could empower anyone to build their own software. Parents could whip up custom apps to help track demanding club sports schedules. Picky eaters could create dynamic meal plans that adapt to whatever’s in their fridge. Polyamorous people could build software to manage their relationship hierarchies. Whatever random, niche software you can imagine, you can build it.

But Osika isn’t satisfied with helping millions of people vibe code apps for their everyday life—he also wants Lovable users to make more cash. The startup claims that around 80 percent of users arrive at the platform with a financial incentive, like building customer-facing platforms for online sales. That said, Lovable also reports that only 35 percent currently earn revenue with their projects.

That brings us back to the cake question. Lovable’s plan for next year is to help you run a small business based on your passions, like opening a cake shop. Fabian Hedin, Lovable’s other cofounder and chief technology officer, says the startup is building automations to help with everything from initial business strategy and website creation to long-term customer retention and marketing plans.

For example, a cake shop owner receives an AI-generated morning briefing through a chatbot-style, Lovable dashboard. “You set some goals, and then the AI is proactive in helping you reach those goals,” Hedin says. This briefing analyzes the number of cake boxes sold through a holiday promotion, customer emails it automatically answered, and reminders to make financial deposits on time.

Lovable has been a boon for savvy social media content creators, who can leverage their platforms better through vibe-coded sites. “People who have audiences themselves are building larger businesses around that,” Osika says. He recently went to a dinner in New York with creators, one of whom uses Lovable to help sell their book. Others have used it to help hawk merch.

Lovable earning the trust of burgeoning entrepreneurs is critical to the success of this new endeavor, though it may be an uphill battle. Vibe-coded projects were notorious for not necessarily being secure and sometimes exposing user data.

The startup was one of many vibe-coded services that came under fire this year for facilitating user-generated apps that exposed data on the open web. Earlier this month, Lovable revamped its security approach as part of its effort to make sites generated through its platform more secure by default.

“The moment real people use what you build, security is the product,” Igor Andriushchenko, Lovable’s head of security, tells WIRED. “That's why it's one of the areas we continue investing in the most and why we’ve built it directly into the platform experience.”

Osika will see Lovable as successful next year if he can help a new wave of entrepreneurs start sustainable businesses. Why just vibe code an app when you can vibe code a living?

paragraphs: AI-native spend management platform Payhawk has announced US$280m in Series C funding led by Growth Equity of Goldman Sachs Alternatives, bringing its valuation to US$2bn and total funding to more than US$515m.
Payhawk says the Series C capital will be used to pursue building “the global Finance Operating System for the AI era”.
“The US$280m we’ve secured will help us scale globally,” Hristo Borisov, Co-Founder and CEO of Payhawk, tells FinTech Magazine.

“With fintech representing only a small percentage of the global payments market, we, like our investors, see an incredible growth opportunity and room to bring finance teams AI-native products that combine agents, payments infrastructure and enterprise controls."
Payhawk was founded in 2018 with the AI to transform how businesses handle spending and payments.
In 2026, it operates across 33 countries and 12 offices, with a platform spanning multiple currencies, banking systems payment rails, regulations and local practices.
It is this complexity that Hristo believes can become a global advantage: “Europe does not need to build local versions of categories invented somewhere else,” he says.
“We should build categories the rest of the world follows as craftsmanship and innovation are strongly embedded cultural traits for Europeans.”
The ultimate aim, Hristo says, is to build the infrastructure through which global businesses run their financial operations, with AI at the forefront.

“Being born in Europe has exposed us to this complexity from day one. We know what it takes for our customers to stay in control with their businesses spread around the world while scaling and while trying to be efficient at the same time,” Hristo adds.
“The window to define that category is open now, and we are moving fast.”
With Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, the ERP systems, banks, treasury products, procurement platforms, travel tools and spend platforms are all becoming more intelligent.
Yet Payhawk argues that smarter applications do not automatically translate to a smarter finance operation on the whole.
“Integrations connect systems. MCP makes information easier to access. But an operating system changes how the entire finance function works,” Hristo points out.
“As software moves from recommending actions to actually taking them, that distinction becomes much more important.”
That is why Payhawk is building its Finance Operating System around three interconnected layers which allow AI to move beyond simple assistance and become part of the operating model of finance.

The layers include AI agents which perform financial work, payments infrastructure allowing for agents to safely interact with money, and enterprise controls that provide finance teams with governance on what agents can do and when human assistance is needed.
Payhawk says this will align its growth while still allowing its customers to save money instead of incentivising them to spend more.
The independence will also allow Payhawk to develop its AI-native finance suite that work beyond its own cards.

“Payhawk’s exceptional growth reflects the strength of its engineering DNA, global footprint and clear vision for the future of modern spend management systems,” James Hayward, Managing Director within Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, says.
“As payments, AI and enterprise software increasingly converge, we believe Payhawk is well positioned to emerge as a leader in this rapidly evolving market.
“We are excited to partner with the team as they continue to scale globally and enter their next phase of growth.”
James is set to join Payhawk’s Board of Directors following the Series C funding round.

Visa partners with Payhawk as its card network, with Payhawk operating as a Visa principal member under EU and UK electronic money institution licences. That status underpins Payhawk’s corporate Visa cards, which sit alongside its expense management, accounts payable, budgeting and procurement tools in a single platform for finance teams.

Oracle NetSuite integrates with Payhawk through a native connector available on the NetSuite SuiteApp Marketplace. Payhawk reports that 99.7% of transactions sync with zero manual intervention and that customers close their books 50% faster. The link gives enterprise finance teams live, two-way data flow with their ERP.

Sage Intacct lists Payhawk as a recommended solution on its marketplace following the integration’s launch on 10 September 2024. Multi-entity finance customers can connect all legal entities to Sage Intacct in a single setup, which supports Payhawk’s push into international markets.

news.title: Anthropic IPO set to deliver windfall to handful of smaller VC firms
news.title_en: Anthropic IPO set to deliver windfall to handful of smaller VC firms

inline_images.caption: Manager of pop superstar Madonna, Guy Oseary, stands to net more than $7bn from an early investment of just over $400mn © Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg
inline_images.alt: Manager of pop superstar Madonna, Guy Oseary, stands to net more than $7bn from an early investment of just over $400mn © Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg

news.author: George Hammond
news.content_snippet: Small group of lesser-known firms primed for returns at multiples that would surpass larger, blue-chip rivals.
news.summary_en: AI startup Anthropic is preparing for its IPO with an expected valuation of $1.4 trillion, set to deliver over $100 billion in combined returns to early-stage venture capital firms including Spark Capital and Factorial Funds. Post-IPO, Amazon and Google will collectively control nearly 30% of the company, while major investors like Iconiq Capital, Lightspeed Ventures, and Menlo Ventures see their stakes reach multi-billion dollar valuations.
news.article_content_en:
Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday will reorder Silicon Valley’s power rankings, with a small group of venture capitalists who bet early and aggressively on the AI lab set for a combined windfall of well over $100bn.

Anthropic is expected to be valued at $1.4tn or more when it lists. That would be about 2,300 times its value when Anjney Midha — an angel investor and founder of AMP PBC — first backed the company in 2021.

His firm is among a handful of lesser-known groups primed for massive returns at multiples that would surpass those of larger, blue-chip rivals. Others include Spark Capital, which would own about $11bn of stock at a $1.4tn valuation, and Factorial Funds, which would own just over $10bn, according to FT calculations.

Spark’s Yasmin Razavi and Factorial’s Sol Bier invested in Anthropic’s series C funding round, which closed in 2023, when the company was valued at about $4bn. Razavi sits on Anthropic’s board.

Meanwhile, the manager of pop superstar Madonna, Guy Oseary, stands to net more than $7bn from an early investment of just over $400mn.

“The deck chairs are shifting around in the VC landscape,” said a partner at one midsized VC firm which stands to make billions of dollars. “The leaders in the AI wave are not the same as they were in the previous waves. Different firms are moving up the leaderboard, and we’re glad to be among them.”

Amazon and Google, which have provided investment and computing resources to Anthropic, will collectively own close to 30 per cent of the company after the IPO.

The largest financial investor in the company, Iconiq Capital, holds a fraction of that. Nevertheless, its stake would be worth about $28bn at a $1.4tn valuation. It is followed by Lightspeed Ventures — which has invested roughly $3.2bn for a stake worth just over $25bn at the same valuation — and Menlo Ventures, which stands to return $21bn from an initial $1bn investment.

Coatue and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC invested later but went big. The pair led a funding round earlier this year which valued Anthropic at $380bn, and have each put close to $5bn into the company. Those stakes would be worth more than $10bn at an IPO price of $1.4tn.

Sound Ventures, which was founded by Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, and Bessemer Venture Partners are each poised for returns of about $7bn. For Bessemer, that would mark an eightfold increase on its initial investment, while Sound stands to make roughly 17 times its outlay.

Even those massive multiples are dwarfed, though, by the roughly 70-times return jailed crypto exchange founder Sam Bankman-Fried would have made if his company had not been forced to sell its $500mn stake in bankruptcy proceedings in 2024. That stake would be worth about $35bn at an IPO price of $1.4tn.

The clamour to own a stake in the AI company has increased in the past year, as the group’s revenues have leapfrogged rival OpenAI. A partner at one of Anthropic’s large investors said they “wrote [chief financial officer Krishna Rao] a love letter” as they jostled for access to a funding round earlier this year.

The take-off prompted OpenAI’s investors, including Brad Gerstner’s Altimeter, Sequoia Capital and Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund, to pour money into Anthropic, an unusual move in Silicon Valley, where VCs tend to back a single company in each field and founders prize fealty.

Other big-name venture firms, including Thrive Capital and Andreessen Horowitz, skipped Anthropic entirely.

“Call us old school . . . but we are serial monogamists,” said Josh Kushner, founder of Thrive, which is one of OpenAI’s largest and most vocal backers, in a since-deleted post on X.

Andreessen’s partners and Anthropic’s executives, meanwhile, have clashed over how best to regulate AI.

A successful IPO would also make thousands of Anthropic employees multimillionaires.

However, the company’s executives have framed fundraising as a necessary evil in the pursuit of their mission to responsibly “develop advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity”.

While its investors celebrate once-in-a-lifetime returns, Anthropic’s leadership is plotting a low-key IPO. The company has no plans for a party to celebrate the listing and intends to keep fanfare around what is set to be the biggest listing fundraise of all time to a minimum, said people with knowledge of the matter.

news.article_content_en:
Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company’s vision for its new “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.”

The announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent’s work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.

The rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the company first announced in September. Parts of that vision are now becoming “generally available,” as Nadella puts it, with autonomous agents and new governance tools arriving alongside them.

### All about agents

Copilot Autopilot (not to be confused with Windows Autopilot) is a “persistent, proactive agent for personal productivity” according to Microsoft. In a nutshell, Autopilot is a cloud-based autonomous AI agent that users can delegate responsibilities to, not just single tasks. Autopilot can be authorized to work across services like email and calendars and complete tasks assigned to it as part of its role. Autopilot will use usage-based billing via Copilot Credits, but final pricing has not been announced ahead of general availability.

Also announced as generally available at the keynote speech was Microsoft IQ, an intelligence platform that houses Work IQ, a context layer that helps agents understand a company’s communications, relationships, and ongoing work. Nadella described Work IQ as perhaps a company’s most valuable database: “It has a deep understanding of the people, their relationships to other people, your emails, your meetings, chats, projects that make up all the fabric of work.” Whether companies want autonomous agents to have access to internal documents and messaging data will have to be determined by their own internal IT review.

Copilot Workspaces is a collaborative environment currently available through Microsoft’s Frontier early-access program, but coming soon will be the ability to bring personal Autopilot agents into Workspaces. Early in the keynote address, Nadella said that “Until now, AI interactions have mostly been single-player. Workspaces makes it a truly multiplayer experience, where people and agents drive towards a common goal, with shared context.”

### Governance over trust

Trust, the third pillar of Microsoft’s new frontier ecosystem, was something that Nadella continued returning to during his presentation, and not in a way that some might expect. “We find ourselves in a place where alignment is elusive. Mechanistic understanding of these models is elusive. The question is: How can you even trust all this powerful technology? The reality is, by definition, you can’t,” he said.

In a departure from the norms of “AI is magic” corporate hype sentiment, Nadella conceded that the internal workings of AI thought processes remain difficult to understand, and models cannot be trusted to govern themselves, regardless of whether their answers are accurate. Nadella described the solution as “an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence” from the authority granted to it. Microsoft says each Autopilot agent will have a unique ID, and administrators can restrict permissions or block it entirely. All agent activities are logged for human review, and Autopilot can ask for human approval before engaging in certain actions.

The promised agent controls and admission that AI systems can’t always be trusted are meaningful, but Microsoft is asking businesses and users to place their trust in the company’s own safeguards instead, though the effectiveness of those safeguards against mistakes, rogue actions, or data exposure will still have to be demonstrated. In Microsoft’s view, the solution to untrustworthy intelligence is not to make AI agents trustworthy, but to control what they’re permitted to do. Businesses will have to decide how much autonomy they delegate to agents.

Along with the guardrails, Microsoft announced what it calls the “AI Transparency Initiative.” The effort has partnered with 40-plus major companies, including Adobe and Mastercard, to develop open, industrywide standards for AI governance and security. Nadella described the initiative as a way for industry to “help establish an open standard that makes AI safer, more transparent, and more accessible.”

### Minding and measuring token-spend

Along with the other announced additions, Microsoft also announced expanding capabilities for Agent 365, its existing control plane for managing AI agents across enterprise environments. The new agent sheriff extends existing identity, security, and management systems to AI agents. Microsoft describes the objective as providing “observability at every layer of the stack.” Agent 365 offers governance controls over agent behavior in what Microsoft says is “autonomous in execution, but bounded and supervised.”

Along with Agent 365 comes Agent 365 Business Analytics: “You can simply think of this as an ERP system of AI usage. You can see exactly what’s driving the spend and connect the spend to the outcomes that drive business value,” said Nadella. Customers will be able to see real-world costs associated with AI token-spend, and compare those metrics to the value of work performed. Microsoft acknowledged that the estimations of assisted work hours are determined by a model, and not a direct measurement of time that may have been saved. This is a telling concession for Microsoft to make as businesses evaluate whether there will be an ROI on AI implementations, but according to Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft Commercial Business, “anything you can do with Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot, for less.”

### The outage in the room

Nadella offered only a brief acknowledgment of last week’s outage that disrupted access to services like Exchange Online and Teams for users across the globe. “Last week was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world,” he said. “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously, and in that context I know we have work to do.”

That statement was all the time the elephant in the room was given, but Microsoft did seem to acknowledge the public’s growing concern over data center projects by highlighting the previously discussed “community-first AI infrastructure plan.” Not a surprise in a presentation that asks organizations to extend more autonomy to software agents, at a time when Microsoft’s existing infrastructure is under increased scrutiny.

[Root Cause & Mechanism] To analyze the correlation between digital social habits and mental well-being
[Key Metrics] Prevalence reaches 50% among daily users, linked to higher risk of loneliness.
[Key Position & Outlook] In-person friendships remain superior for emotional support compared to digital-only modes.
news.article_content_en:
As generational cohorts go, Gen Z has been saddled with its share of labels. They scarcely have sex, are “quiet quitters” when it comes to office jobs, and, as they avoid traditional partnership, have learned to solomaxx.

Whether these labels are deserved or completely off the mark, what continually connects this unique class of young people is a desire to reconstruct how they think about connection.

In “Friendship in an Online-Offline World: Digital Life, Connection and Wellbeing” researchers from public polling firm Gallup and the Digital Wellness Lab at Boston Children’s Hospital found that more than one-third of Gen Z (33 percent) rely on AI for companionship. The percentage was higher among daily AI users, spiking to 50 percent, and 42 percent among those with online-only friends.

Rather than measure the consequences of screen time alone, the report examines who Gen Z connects with and how those relationships not only account for their social lives but also how they impact their mental health. While in-person friendships were rated the highest for “strength and support” and were “associated with the most positive emotional experiences,” young people who rely on online-only friends or AI as a social companion may have higher odds of loneliness than those who do not.

Researchers examined three modes of what they consider close connection: in-person friendships, friendships that started IRL but are sustained online, and online-only friendships where a young person has never met their friend in real life. The survey, conducted between May and August, sampled 15,925 people aged 15 to 22 across 16 countries, and suggests that Gen Z benefits more from IRL relationships compared to digital ones, despite nearly half of young people in the US having at least one close online-only friend.

“Adolescence is a time when you thrive when you socialize, and so they’re looking for all of these contexts to socialize in,” says David Bickham, research director of the Digital Wellness Lab. “I don’t necessarily see it as, oh, these kids have some sort of major deficit and are looking to AI. I see it as these are young people who are growing up in a time of AI, the most powerful way to find information online, and the more they use it, they see and are more engaged with the social side of it.”

While AI may help fill a genuine social gap, it hasn’t yet taken the place of their IRL bonds. “In-person and digitally mediated friendships coexist within the same social life,” write the authors of the report.

When it comes to maintaining those affiliations, Instagram and Discord—surprisingly, not TikTok—were the top platforms in the US for staying in touch with online-only friends. Bickham also noted that “loneliness specifically may be something that these online relationships can’t quite compensate for.”

“Kids who are reporting loneliness really do things online that are consistent with trying to make friends. They talk to people they don't know, which is always a risk, but it’s also how you make friends,” Bickham says. The report found that Gen Z men, who were more likely to have digital friendships than women, often encountered new acquaintances through gaming, while young women mentioned social media as their most common category to cultivate connection. “What’s intriguing is that boys who are higher in social anxiety are less likely to make connections. They tend to do things by themselves, but when it comes to AI, what we found is that kids who are still lonely are going to seek out connections” with chatbots, Bickham says.

Recent debates over teen screen time have centered on whether digital devices are driving a youth mental health crisis or if the concerns are overstated. Some critics believe that by only measuring screen time it overlooks the type of content young people watch. This year, social media bans and age-restriction policies for minors took effect in Australia and the UK. In the US, where state legislators have introduced bills to curb addictive design features, a majority of Americans support banning kids under 16 from using social media, according to a recent Pew Research survey.

Jon-Patrick Allem, an associate professor at the Rutgers School of Public Health, wrote last year in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine that research on the topic has primarily focused on “blunt measures of screen time” and that doing so would “treat all content consumed online as uniform.” Allem concluded that this approach is “deficient” and called on researchers to set a new agenda that instead investigates the actual content kids were consuming, not just time spent.

It was also important to Bickham and his team to look beyond a surface-level analysis of screen time and consider the nature of the relationships being formed while young people were online, zeroing in on how that time is spent and who it’s spent with.

“It’s very difficult to measure screen time accurately in a survey. Mainly because half the kids told us this was something they’re doing all the time. A more important finding is the quality of relationship. It’s how you use these platforms that’s going to dictate your outcome, not just how long you use them for.”

A previous report from the Digital Wellness Lab mapped the use of AI among teenagers in the US, Brazil, and France and found that teens aged 13 to 17 were turning to AI for personal advice and creative work, in addition to companionship.

While researchers are wary of classifying the report as a permanent shift in how young people form relationships, they say it does signal a growing reliance on AI companionship as part of a pattern of digital social engagement unfolding among Gen Z.

“It wouldn’t be surprising if AI companionship becomes more common over the next five years as AI becomes integrated into young people’s everyday lives,” says Andrew Dugan, a principal researcher at Gallup. “But whether young people are turning to AI because they feel lonely, or whether AI companionship might reinforce those feelings, remains an important question for future research.”

news.title: YouTube found a new way to inflate view counts
news.title_en: YouTube found a new way to inflate view counts
news.author: Emma Roth
news.content_snippet:
YouTube’s view counts will now include the number of people that it estimates are watching a video together on TV. In an update on Monday, the platform says it’s bringing “co-views” to public view counts across long-form videos, Shorts, and live content to provide a more “complete picture” of how people are using its platform.

YouTube, which has become even more popular on TVs than phones, also says the change will help it align with “TV industry standards,” which similarly record views by esti
news.summary_en: YouTube has introduced 'co-viewing' metrics for TV-based content, including long-form, Shorts, and live streams, by using a privacy-safe statistical model to estimate multiple viewers per device. This move aligns the platform with traditional TV industry standards, relies on demographic data rather than hardware sensors, and does not impact creator monetization.
news.article_content_en:
YouTube’s view counts will now include the number of people that it estimates are watching a video together on TV. In an update on Monday, the platform says it’s bringing “co-views” to public view counts across long-form videos, Shorts, and live content to provide a more “complete picture” of how people are using its platform.

YouTube, which has become even more popular on TVs than phones, also says the change will help it align with “TV industry standards,” which similarly record views by estimating the number of people watching shows. The company says it doesn’t use devices, like cameras or microphones, to estimate how many people are watching a video on TV. Instead, it estimates co-views using a “privacy safe statistical model” that takes into account “demographic patterns and viewing times.”

This marks yet another update to YouTube’s view count system. In August, the platform began counting a view as soon as a video starts playing. The company said at the time that creators will notice their view counts increasing faster as a result of this change, and it seems like adding co-views could boost these numbers as well.

YouTube notes that it will only apply co-views to new views on TV going forward, and that they won’t appear retroactively. Co-views also won’t affect a creator’s ad revenue, YouTube Partner Program eligibility, or revenue.

news.title: LanceDB raises $57.5M to accelerate AI model training with multimodal data platform
news.title_en: LanceDB raises $57.5M to accelerate AI model training with multimodal data platform
news.author: Kyt Dotson
news.content_snippet:
LanceDB Inc., the developer of database technology designed to speed up artificial intelligence models, today announced it has raised $57.5 million in early-stage funding to bring a multimodal lakehouse to researchers, model builders and platform teams.

Bessemer Venture Partners and Innovation Endeavors led the Series B round. Other investors in the round included Theory Ventures, Dimension, Swift Ventures, CRV and Y Combinator, bringing the company’s total funding to $98.5 million.

Built on the open-source Lance format, the company provides a multimodal data lakehouse that unifies structured and unstructured data, addressing infrastructure bottlenecks in AI training workflows.

Prosecutors accuse Huawei of scheming to defraud HSBC and other banks about its business in Iran and conspiring to steal trade secrets from five US tech companies. It was also indicted as a criminal enterprise.

news.summary_en: US federal prosecutors accused Huawei of a 20-year scheme to defraud financial institutions regarding its Iran operations and conspiring to steal trade secrets from five American tech firms, characterizing it as a criminal enterprise. Huawei's defense lawyer, Brian Heberlig, countered in closing arguments that the prosecution failed to prove its charges, asserting that the banks were aware of the risks and that Huawei's market success was earned through innovation rather than illicit activities.
news.article_content_en:
Prosecutors accuse Huawei of scheming to defraud HSBC and other banks about its business in Iran and conspiring to steal trade secrets from five US tech companies. It was also indicted as a criminal enterprise.

“They began with guilt and worked backwards,” defense lawyer Brian Heberlig told jurors in Brooklyn federal court in his closing argument. “When the evidence didn’t fit its theory, it moved the goal posts,” he said.

The government offered jurors a very different picture of the company on Monday, and said prosecutors proved beyond a reasonable doubt that Huawei operated as a criminal enterprise.

“For 20 years, Huawei committed a pattern of crimes targeted at American companies, the American financial system and the American government,” prosecutor Meredith Arfa said in her closing statement. “It is time to finally hold Huawei accountable,” Arfa said.

However, Heberlig argued the banks all knew Huawei operated in Iran, which is under US sanctions. He said the banks accepted the risk and competed for Huawei’s business.

In relation to the alleged theft of trade secrets, “the government cherry-picked a handful of incidents … and tried to convert them into a 20-year conspiracy,” Heberlig said.

“Huawei didn’t steal its way to success,” he said. “It earned it, plain and simple,” he added.

The Huawei case burst into the headlines in 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, its CFO and daughter of the founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant for her role in the alleged bank fraud.

She entered into an agreement with prosecutors in 2021 and the charges against her were dismissed, but the case dragged on.

The jury is likely to begin deliberations on Wednesday. The case went to trial in September. The prosecution put on over 60 witnesses, and the defence about 15.

The jury will deliver its verdict as US-China tensions heat up in the battle over artificial intelligence and amid a fragile trade truce between the two countries.

inline_images.caption: Bloomberg/Getty Images Michael Burry, the investor of "The Big Short" fame.
inline_images.alt: Bloomberg/Getty Images Michael Burry, the investor of "The Big Short" fame.

news.author: Bloomberg
news.content_snippet:
Michael Burry says Anthropic's IPO filing this week has reinforced his concerns that the entire AI ecosystem is at risk of disaster. The investor of "The Big Short" fame wrote in a Substack post on Tuesday that the first in-depth look at Claude's parent company, ahead of what could be the biggest IPO in history, threw up a bunch of red flags.

Burry pointed to Anthropic's huge spending commitments, slowing revenue, and tangled ties. He said that Anthropic has struck deals to buy about $537 billi
news.summary_en: Investor Michael Burry, analyzing Anthropic's S-1 filing, identified $537 billion in compute procurement commitments to hyperscalers like Amazon, Alphabet, and Microsoft, representing 12 times its annual run-rate revenue. Burry warned that these complex financing loops, involving vendor financing and structured credit, create systemic fragility, suggesting that any deceleration in AI demand could trigger catastrophic debt defaults across the ecosystem.
news.article_content_en:
Michael Burry says Anthropic's IPO filing this week has reinforced his concerns that the entire AI ecosystem is at risk of disaster. The investor of "The Big Short" fame wrote in a Substack post on Tuesday that the first in-depth look at Claude's parent company, ahead of what could be the biggest IPO in history, threw up a bunch of red flags.

Burry pointed to Anthropic's huge spending commitments, slowing revenue, and tangled ties. He said that Anthropic has struck deals to buy about $537 billion of compute from the likes of Amazon, Alphabet, and Microsoft, and reached preliminary agreements worth hundreds of billions more with others such as SpaceXAI, putting its total commitments at about 12 times its current annual run-rate revenue.

"This is not stated clearly in the S-1, and in my view it is the most deserved headline from it," Burry wrote in a Tuesday Substack post. He underscored how hyperscalers like Amazon and Alphabet act as Anthropic's "lenders, vendors, channel providers, and shareholders." He also outlined its deal with Broadcom, which involves Apollo and Blackstone and includes convertible notes and structured credit tranches.

"Just remember, the reason this is so complex is because too much debt is needed, and it must be unloaded from the balance sheets of those involved," Burry wrote. "While some may see all the circularity and connectedness as security on the way up, and that is not wrong, it does leave the entire organism catastrophically vulnerable either on a pause or on the way down," he added.

He also described financing arrangements in the AI space as "garish and audacious," and said hyperscalers aren't generating enough cash to fund the AI buildout so they're resorting to "Byzantine" deals. Burry said it was a "very similar" situation with vendor financing during the dot-com bubble, saying "people keep making the same mistakes with every new thing." In its filing, Anthropic said its revenue surpassed $16 billion for the first six months of this year, a 14-fold increase from the first half of 2025.

Its operating loss narrowed by about two-thirds to below $700 million, and it generated nearly $4 billion in operating cash flow. Burry initially commented on Anthropic's filing in a Substack chat thread on Monday. He said that revenue was "slowing," citing Anthropic's claim that third-quarter revenue was 86 times the $197 million it generated in the fourth quarter of 2024, or about $16.9 billion.

That would mean Anthropic's revenue grew by about 46% between the second and third quarters of this year, after soaring 144% between the first and second quarters. "Overall slowing of growth is not attributed to a decline in tokenmaxxing, but I did not expect that to be mentioned," Burry wrote.

Burry was referring to the trend of maximizing AI token consumption, which has fallen out of favor in recent months given its costs. In another comment, Burry wrote that large language models (LLMs) like Claude are "improving" and "already being used more efficiently and that trend will continue, to the detriment of their growth rate." Burry said he's focused on the complexity and fragility of the debt financing many AI deals, hurdles to installing new graphics chips shoring up demand for older chips, a potential crash in memory chip prices once the shortage eases, compression and small language models (SLMs) reducing the need for computing power, and the "fundamentals behind not just companies but the deals they are doing." Responding to a subscriber who said that Big Tech companies are shifting from Anthropic's AI models to their own, and that tokens are rapidly being commoditized, Burry wrote: "Yes, that is what I hear." Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Burry's posts.

The contrarian investor shot to fame after his massive wager against the mid-2000s housing bubble was chronicled in the book and movie "The Big Short." He pivoted from running a hedge fund to writing about his personal investments on Substack last winter. A recurring theme of his work since then has been deep skepticism of the AI boom.

He's flagged slowing growth, overinvestment in microchips and data centers, aggressive accounting, hidden liabilities, and circular financing deals.

news.article_content_en:
Wall Street executives and the National Security Agency have told members of Congress that this week’s widespread tech outages were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities identified by artificial intelligence, according to three sources familiar with the private conversations.

Over the last few days, the country has faced a series of startling tech failures, leading to a pause in all flights nationwide, customers being unable to access their bank accounts and a highly classified communications network at the National Security Agency going down.

While it does not appear that these disruptions were caused by a cyberattack, government and banking officials have told lawmakers that they stem from attempts to fix gaps in cyber defenses identified by AI models, the sources said. The fixes, however, temporarily overwhelmed the systems.

“These models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, and that increases the urgency to patch right away,” said one congressional official briefed on the matter. “They’re trying to push through a lot of patches all at once — more than the system was designed for.”

On Monday, banks such as JP Morgan Chase blamed software-related bugs for the service issues. On Tuesday, the NSA said that “scheduled routine maintenance” was responsible for the “temporary degradation” of some of its networks. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told CNBC on Tuesday that “they’re pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system. ... We’re going to see more of this as new technology rolls out.”

Powerful companies and government agencies have increasingly trained the most powerful AI models on themselves, seeking to identify the vulnerabilities that others may weaponize against them. Once these gaps are identified, they are under immense pressure to patch them as soon as possible, knowing that malicious actors have access to comparable AI tools — or will soon.

This urgency is what has driven a wide range of public- and private-sector actors to rush fixes to their systems faster than they normally would, the sources said. But even entities with large resources, such as the nation’s top banks and the intelligence community, are finding it difficult to do so without accidentally causing outages. The sources spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations.

The outages rippled across the country this week. The Federal Aviation Administration canceled more than 20,000 flights as a result of the nationwide ground stop, according to The Wall Street Journal. Microsoft experienced a major outage of Outlook.

Microsoft blamed a technical defect for the disruption. It is also unclear what caused the FAA systems to go down.

“There’s some sense in which this is reassuring, in that it means there’s not an attack. But it shows the extent to which safety critical infrastructure we rely on is based on software with large vulnerabilities on legacy systems,” said Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at Encode. “Updating those is going to be a rocky process, and as we get more advanced models this won’t be a one and done thing — we’ll continue to find more vulnerabilities.”

The NSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The malfunctions have undermined confidence in key systems used for essential tasks.

SAN FRANCISCO – Technology failures disrupting everything from Americans’ air travel and banking transactions to secretive work at the US National Security Agency are fuelling public distrust and paranoia about ageing tech infrastructure – even with no sign the episodes are linked or the work of malicious actors.

Breakdowns over the past week have caused enough havoc to spur American consumers into a panic-buy
news.summary_en: Recent high-profile system outages across the NSA, FAA, and Microsoft have paralyzed essential services, fueling public anxiety despite no evidence of malicious cyber-attacks. Senator Mark Warner emphasized that AI-driven vulnerability discovery is forcing organizations to push updates at an unsustainable pace, exposing the systemic fragility of aging digital infrastructure.
news.article_content_en:
The malfunctions have undermined confidence in key systems used for essential tasks.

SAN FRANCISCO – Technology failures disrupting everything from Americans’ air travel and banking transactions to secretive work at the US National Security Agency are fuelling public distrust and paranoia about ageing tech infrastructure – even with no sign the episodes are linked or the work of malicious actors.

Breakdowns over the past week have caused enough havoc to spur American consumers into a panic-buying spree.

At Costco Wholesale Corp, surging purchases of non-perishable foods, water and battery supplies led analysts to increase its share price target to US$1,150 from US$1,100.

Most of the company’s high-ticket generators were sold out online as of Nov 15.

Late night comedians have also feasted on the tech-related turmoil: Saturday Night Live dedicated its cold open over the weekend to a faux CIA meeting where an agent played by comedian John Mulaney used problems at the Federal Aviation Administration and Microsoft Corp as a punchline.

It’s unusual and concerning to have so many high-profile incidents clustered so closely together, said Joe Slowik, director of threat research and cyber engineering at the risk intelligence firm Dataminr.

“We have become far too reliant on infrastructure that is shaky being more available than it is,” he said.

While there was no public indication that the computer breakdowns were related or the work of hackers, taken together, they touch on the broader anxieties surrounding artificial intelligence, including the possibility that AI tools could make it easier for malicious actors to knock out essential services or conduct cybercrime sprees.

In statement addressing the outages, Senator Mark Warner, Democrat from Virginia, said it appears they are the “consequence of how quickly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape.”

“AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” Warner said.

In the latest glitch, a classified computer network that the NSA uses for internal communications went down on Nov 17, leaving some staff unable to access workplace systems, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The issue resulted in the NSA telling some personnel to delay their arrival at the agency’s headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland, the person said.

Computer troubles at the spy agency were joined by outages on Nov 17 on some Apple Inc platforms, the latest in a series of breakdowns that also hobbled Microsoft’s software and snarled air traffic nationwide over the past several days.

While the Trump administration has been quick to say that the incidents were technical failures and not the work of hackers, the malfunctions have nonetheless undermined confidence in key systems used for essential tasks.

The episodes on Nov 17 capped a week of similar problems elsewhere, including a technical lapse at Chase on Nov 16 that caused some customers’ transactions to take longer to process.

The issue wasn’t related to a cybersecurity event, the bank said, but tied to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems.

United Airlines also said on Nov 16 that a tech issue impacted its departing flights, and that the problem was traced to equipment problems involving the agency’s aging communications infrastructure.

A lack of quick and clear answers about the events created opportunities for conspiracy theorists and unreliable social media influencers to capitalise.

Some viral posts suggested the US was under a coordinated attack from a foreign – or extraterrestrial – government.

Others warned that the tech disruptions signalled a kind of warning for a vague future cataclysm.

At Apple, the company is working to restore its systems after an internal update caused wide-scale outages Nov 17, disrupting employee tools, retail operations and consumer services.

The malfunction knocked out several internal services, including AppleWeb, the employee portal, AppleConnect, the internal sign-in system, and virtual private network access for remote workers, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

Microsoft’s productivity software was hobbled for a more extended period last week after a bug caused a systems malfunction during an otherwise routine rerouting of user traffic.

And US air traffic experienced its worst weekend in decades after a government contractor tried to replace outdated copper wire at a remote location in Arkansas, causing a router to overwhelm others on the air traffic control network with excessive connection requests.

The Trump administration is under pressure for more answers to the rapid-fire series of glitches.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told CNBC that the recent technology failures weren’t the result of a cyberattack, while President Donald Trump sought to play down the significance of the malfunctions after being asked about them during his trip to Asia.

“It’s going to be very much under control. It’s life,” Trump said on Nov 17 when questioned about the outages at Chase and Microsoft. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

Even as the administration sought to offer assurances about the malfunctions, the Federal Bureau of Investigation issued a warning that cyber criminals and state-backed hackers are seeking to use artificial intelligence-powered tools to automate attacks on companies and other organsations worldwide.

A Quinnipiac University poll released in September found that 73% of Americans were concerned that future systems could pose an existential threat to humanity.

Nearly eight in 10 of those surveyed said they favoured slowing or stopping AI development altogether to better understand the safety risks.

Despite public misgivings about the risks posed by artificial intelligence, major technology companies are racing to use AI to discover and plug holes in their systems.

AI tools have already finding record numbers of software flaws, though tech firms say they are largely finding those issues themselves, rather than learning about them when hackers try exploiting them in attacks.

For instance, Alphabet Inc.’s Google said in July that it discovered 433 bugs in its Google Chrome browser versus 11 in an equivalent update the year before.

Of those, 401 were reported by Google internally, according to the company.

Still, in June, the National Security Agency and the intelligence services of other nations in the “Five Eyes” alliance published a joint advisory urging organisations to, among other things, accelerate their software-patching practices.

“AI is shortening the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation,” the agencies wrote. “Delays in patching increase risk, especially for operational systems with long update cycles.”

Christiaan Beek of the cybersecurity firm Rapid7 Inc cautioned that nothing in the public record about the latest outages suggests they were the result of rushed security updates.

In general, he said that organisations face major risks in relying on outdated processes to respond to the surge in AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and the resulting patches.

“Complex systems fail in boring ways far more often than because of an adversary,” he said.

“The boring reason isn’t harmless, though, and worryingly, it means the systems we rely on are fragile enough that we can bring them down ourselves, no attackers needed.”

The failure of the FAA’s flight-control system on Nov 13 apparently involved the replacement of an old telecommunications cable that triggered a cascade of errors involving a roughly 25-year-old network router.

Experts say that network equipment such as routers can be finicky and surprisingly fragile technologies, as small errors or glitches can cause them to go haywire and either fail or flood their networks with traffic.

In the wake of the FAA failures, the Trump administration is seeking US$50.1 billion (S$64.57 billion) to overhaul the US airspace system, citing an “urgent need” to modernise the critical infrastructure, though the effort is already facing objections in the Senate.

“We have underinvested in redundancy – whether it’s an error, an update that went wrong, even a cyber incident – that can step in to ensure worst case scenarios don’t happen,” said Slowik. BLOOMBERG

news.title: F.A.A. Shelves Routers Like the One Linked to the Nationwide Ground Stop
news.title_en: F.A.A. Shelves Routers Like the One Linked to the Nationwide Ground Stop
news.author: Neil Vigdor
news.content_snippet: Federal officials said they believed that a router made by Juniper Networks caused a data overload that disrupted communications.
news.summary_en: The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has suspended the installation and operation of Juniper Networks routers, following findings that a recently installed unit in El Dorado, Arkansas, contributed to last week's nationwide air traffic control ground stop. Despite Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) asserting no defects, the incident, coupled with recent outages at the National Security Agency's classified communications network, highlights mounting concerns over the resilience of critical infrastructure supply chains and maintenance protocols.
news.article_content_en:
The Federal Aviation Administration has suspended its installation of routers like the one that transportation officials said they believed had contributed to a nationwide ground stop on Friday after it overloaded communications systems used by air traffic controllers and pilots.

The broadcasting function of more than 60 other identical devices on the network was disabled after the disruptions wreaked havoc on air travel, according to the F.A.A., which said on Tuesday that the changes had taken effect in quick succession in response to the chain of events on Friday.

Made by Juniper Networks, which was acquired last year by Hewlett Packard Enterprise, the routers were intended to replace older Cisco Systems models as part of a sweeping program by the F.A.A. to modernize its equipment.

For decades, copper wiring has been the backbone of that antiquated system, which the federal government has slowly started to replace with modern fiber-optic cables.

But while an engineer was installing one of the replacement routers on Friday at an F.A.A. radio center in El Dorado, Ark., data began flooding the network, overwhelming the system and hampering communications, federal officials said. That engineer was working for L3Harris, the company that owns the network used by the F.A.A., and was being monitored by an F.A.A. technician, officials said.

A second router at an F.A.A. radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, also became unstable, according to the F.A.A., which said technicians had resolved the problem by disabling both routers.

“So we thought it’s only prudent to pause the use of these routers,” Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said at a news conference on Tuesday on Capitol Hill.

Mr. Duffy suggested the router glitch was isolated, saying that federal officials had grounded flights out of an abundance of caution.

“Sixty-eight times it worked well,” he said earlier in the news conference. “This one router started to broadcast into our network, and it started to overload the network.”

Federal transportation officials said on Tuesday that the replacement routers had been tested for a year before being installed.

“We don’t know the fault trigger,” Bryan Bedford, the F.A.A. administrator, said at the news conference. “We do know that this router could be enabled to do what it did.”

In a statement on Tuesday, Adam Bauer, a spokesman for Hewlett Packard Enterprise, disputed that the Juniper Networks device was defective.

“Based on what we know and have been told by others, our equipment was working as configured,” Mr. Bauer said. “The F.A.A. is assessing the configuration and performance of all infrastructure involved to determine the cause.”

On Monday, Democratic members of the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee sent a letter to Mr. Duffy and Mr. Bedford urging them to pause the use of the Juniper Networks routers.

“Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed,” the senators wrote. “F.A.A. must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues.”

On Tuesday, federal officials were less measured in their assessment of the performance of L3Harris, which Mr. Duffy said had held contracts with the F.A.A. for more than 20 years and was responsible for monitoring the network.

“They didn’t identify and isolate,” he said. “That concerns me. We have to have them perform better.”

A representative for L3Harris on Tuesday referred to a previous statement, which said the company was “supporting the F.A.A. in its investigation.”

While Mr. Duffy said there was no evidence that the system had been hacked, he noted that F.B.I. analysts were examining the router from the F.A.A. radio facility in Arkansas.

Mr. Bedford said that air traffic controllers had never lost contact with planes while the network was experiencing disruptions. He added that the F.A.A. had backup systems in place but that safety was paramount.

“And people can fly with confidence,” he said.

fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] FAA, HPE, Juniper Networks: Suspension and shutdown of Juniper routers pending technical audit
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Direct correlation between the hardware installation and the nationwide grounding of flights
[Key Fact Detail] FAA halts and deactivates Juniper routers installation.
[Key Position & Outlook] NSA network outage occurs simultaneously, prompting heightened critical infrastructure review.
paragraphs: The Federal Aviation Administration has suspended its installation of routers like the one that transportation officials said they believed had contributed to a nationwide ground stop on Friday after it overloaded communications systems used by air traffic controllers and pilots.

The broadcasting function of more than 60 other identical devices on the network was disabled after the disruptions wreaked havoc on air travel, according to the F.A.A., which said on Tuesday that the changes had taken effect in quick succession in response to the chain of events on Friday.

Made by Juniper Networks, which was acquired last year by Hewlett Packard Enterprise, the routers were intended to replace older Cisco Systems models as part of a sweeping program by the F.A.A. to modernize its equipment.
For decades, copper wiring has been the backbone of that antiquated system, which the federal government has slowly started to replace with modern fiber-optic cables.

But while an engineer was installing one of the replacement routers on Friday at an F.A.A. radio center in El Dorado, Ark., data began flooding the network, overwhelming the system and hampering communications, federal officials said. That engineer was working for L3Harris, the company that owns the network used by the F.A.A., and was being monitored by an F.A.A. technician, officials said.
A second router at an F.A.A. radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, also became unstable, according to the F.A.A., which said technicians had resolved the problem by disabling both routers.
“So we thought it’s only prudent to pause the use of these routers,” Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said at a news conference on Tuesday on Capitol Hill.
Mr. Duffy suggested the router glitch was isolated, saying that federal officials had grounded flights out of an abundance of caution.
“Sixty-eight times it worked well,” he said earlier in the news conference. “This one router started to broadcast into our network, and it started to overload the network.”
Federal transportation officials said on Tuesday that the replacement routers had been tested for a year before being installed.
“We don’t know the fault trigger,” Bryan Bedford, the F.A.A. administrator, said at the news conference. “We do know that this router could be enabled to do what it did.”
In a statement on Tuesday, Adam Bauer, a spokesman for Hewlett Packard Enterprise, disputed that the Juniper Networks device was defective.

“Based on what we know and have been told by others, our equipment was working as configured,” Mr. Bauer said. “The F.A.A. is assessing the configuration and performance of all infrastructure involved to determine the cause.”
On Monday, Democratic members of the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee sent a letter to Mr. Duffy and Mr. Bedford urging them to pause the use of the Juniper Networks routers.

“Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed,” the senators wrote. “F.A.A. must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues.”

On Tuesday, federal officials were less measured in their assessment of the performance of L3Harris, which Mr. Duffy said had held contracts with the F.A.A. for more than 20 years and was responsible for monitoring the network.
“They didn’t identify and isolate,” he said. “That concerns me. We have to have them perform better.”
A representative for L3Harris on Tuesday referred to a previous statement, which said the company was “supporting the F.A.A. in its investigation.”
While Mr. Duffy said there was no evidence that the system had been hacked, he noted that F.B.I. analysts were examining the router from the F.A.A. radio facility in Arkansas.

Mr. Bedford said that air traffic controllers had never lost contact with planes while the network was experiencing disruptions. He added that the F.A.A. had backup systems in place but that safety was paramount.
“And people can fly with confidence,” he said.

news.article_content_en:
Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country.

China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks.

Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff.

The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.”

Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely.

Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue.

In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change.

Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China.

That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch.

If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share.

paragraphs: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled, at least when it comes to how AI might make startling changes to the structure of the economy and how politics might change because of it. “I am AGI-pilled in the sense that at an economy level, what is the political economy’s organization around AGI?” he asked at a roundtable discussion following his Microsoft Ignite keynote at the Chase Center in San Francisco.

But Nadella doesn’t think frontier models like Claude are conscious. “I don’t think so,” he said, adding that he follows Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman’s view that companies should not give rights to models and treat them like they might have a moral status, which companies like Anthropic do as a matter of principle. Suleyman has told me he thinks Anthropic’s team has “wireheaded” themselves, and that this approach is dangerous.

Nadella wasn’t quite as firm about it. “It’s a good debate,” he said. “I’m not sort of dogmatic about it. What I’m saying is the most important social technical issue we have to deal with is how do you ensure that an economy can diffuse this technology broadly?”

I asked Nadella how he was thinking about AI after hearing his response to another reporter’s questions about Anthropic releasing more products in its office suite. Nadella talked at length about the potential collapse of the economy and the end of democracy if one AI model were allowed to achieve monopoly status.
“If the Marxist sort of view is that there’s only one firm, then it’s over, right? For all of us.”

“Most people think about this as a competition between tech firms, which of course it will be,” he said. “But remember, the model has no limits. It’ll be a healthcare company. It can be a financial services company. It can be anything if it wants to be. It can take over the government. Thinking of this as some narrow competition between tech firms, of who is going to get to the next trillion dollars of market cap, is one of the strangest, narrowest ways to think about it.”

Nadella went on to say that the very nature of companies stood to be disrupted in the future. “If intelligence has network effects, what is the future of a firm?” he asked. “If the model sees anything and learns it, and essentially all of human capital collapses into token capital, what is the role of a firm and the human capital in a firm? That’s the debate.”

“I think the political economy is going to get more and more interesting in that context. No one — at least in a democracy — can even win an election if this just goes that way, if there’s only capital and there’s no labor. I mean, I don’t know, that’s not an economy.”
“If the Marxist sort of view is that there’s only one firm, then it’s over, right? For all of us. Not just for me. You are also going to somehow be some affiliate of Anthropic.”
Needless to say, this is not how tech CEOs usually talk about the launch of competing spreadsheet software.

Of course, Nadella was also promoting Microsoft’s various AI tools at Ignite, which promise to let enterprise clients pick the most cost-effective models for various tasks, run their own models, and control their own data in different ways. The idea here is that the market will demand many different kinds of models and sovereign data in order to keep control from centralizing, a theme Nadella kept coming back to as we spoke.
“I think that if you believe that the world, the economy needs more than one firm or two firms, then by definition there need to be as many models as firms of some sort,” he said.

news.author: Carsten Frauenheim, Elizabeth Chamberlain, and Shahram Mokhtari
news.content_snippet:
Apple’s first iPad-stuck-to-a-HomePod smarthome hub landed on our teardown table this week, and we figured we knew what we were getting into. We’ve taken apart plenty of iPads and HomePods. And lately, Apple has actually been getting better at making them repairable.

The original HomePod took a hacksaw to open, but by the second generation, we could get inside without destroying anything. Even the notoriously glue-heavy iPad has made progress: easier battery access, replaceable USB-C ports, and
news.summary_en: iFixit's teardown of the Apple HomeView reveals a heavy reliance on structural adhesives for its display, speakers, and logic board, marking a regressive step in modular design. Despite recent improvements in repairability across iPad and HomePod lines, HomeView’s integration forces high-risk disassembly that frequently leads to component failure.
news.title_zh: 苹果HomeView拆解：维修难度大幅回升
news.summary_zh: iFixit拆解显示，苹果新款智能家居设备HomeView内部高度依赖强力胶粘合，维修难度远超近年推出的iPad与HomePod产品线
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】拆解机构iFixit；硬件厂商苹果公司(Apple Inc.)在实验室拆解环境：显示核心组件强力胶固定，维修与拆解难度极高
【起因与机理】苹果在智能家居类新型复合设备的工程设计上优先考虑了极致集成度与工业强度，放弃了近期在便携设备上体现的维修友好型策略
【核心事实细节】HomeView产品采用高强度强力胶封装，维修难度回归苹果早期水平。
【行业影响与走向】苹果在单一产品设计路径上表现出明显的维修策略退步，或影响第三方服务市场。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] iFixit; Apple Inc. (Laboratory teardown): High-strength adhesive usage prevents non-destructive access to display and logic board
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Prioritization of tight integration and structural rigidity over serviceability in the new smart home product architecture
[Key Fact Detail] HomeView uses industrial-grade adhesives, regressing on recent repairability progress.
[Key Position & Outlook] Shift in design strategy highlights potential conflict between tight hardware integration and right-to-repair standards.
